utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start the testimony of you, Mr. Krajisnik, there are a couple of procedural matters which, as I understood, the Defence preferably would deal with prior to starting the examination of Mr. Krajisnik as a witness. Mr. Krajisnik, I take it that you are informed, although most likely not in much detail, about a decision the Chamber has delivered yesterday. There is one part which is of primary importance to you personally, Mr. Krajisnik, that is the ruling of the Chamber on the matter of contact between counsel and you then being a witness during your testimony. And since you have not taken the oath yet and if there is any need to briefly discuss the matter with counsel, we should rather give you an opportunity now before having asked you to make the solemn declaration. Communication is, as always with witnesses, communication is prohibited. You should not speak with anyone with respect to the testimony you have given then or you're about to give. And for that reason, your two privileged communication telephone lines will be interrupted from the 25th of April, that's today, until the end of your testimony. But of course there could be an urgent reason that you would need to contact counsel during the course of your testimony, so the Chamber can then make an exception. But of course, you cannot address counsel to apply for such an exception. Under the circumstances, if you wish to initiate contact with counsel during your testimony, Mr. Krajisnik, you should write a brief note addressed to the Chamber directly stating the reasons for your wish to contact counsel. You can give that note to a security officer, that -- whether you are in the Detention Unit or here at the Tribunal. So that could be a security officer present in court. These brief notes -- oh, there seems to be a problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a -- well, now we have many -- if you would allow me to finish just this portion, then we'll briefly see how we can resolve the technical problems. So you are then supposed to write a brief note, give it to a security officer, then it will be sent for immediate translation so that the Chamber is informed right away on the content of that note. Therefore, you are also invited to keep it as brief as possible because the longer it is, the longer the translation will take. The original note and the translation will be provided to us. The Chamber will then inform the parties that the Chamber has received a request for communication, although not revealing the content of this note. And then we will decide on whether you will be allowed to communicate with the Defence team or members of the Defence team, and we'll issue instructions concerning the communication. That's, therefore, Mr. Krajisnik, will be the procedure if you need to be in touch with counsel. Before I now continue, I'd like to see whether we can resolve the technical problems. The French channel has some unpleasant -- yes, there's quite some rumble on the French channel. And then Judge Canivell has no -- has on his left screen no image. The matter has been resolved by a -- not by a technician. The rumble on the French channel is still there. It could be just one headphone. If some attention could be paid to it that would be appreciated. I'll just look at whether on my French channel it's -- must be -- it's -- I have no problem on the French channel, so it must be -- okay. All the technical matters having been resolved, I have a short list of procedural matters. The parties have received a copy of my, I would say, agenda, five items on it, procedural matters. Before we start with that, is there any other matter to be added to this short agenda? I see Mr. Harmon nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not on that particular agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter which you would like to prefer to deal with first?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then deal before one moves on to what I might call those housekeeping procedural-type matters in that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I make a couple of submissions, Your Honour. First of all, in relation to the order generally which we received yesterday evening, we can see a number of points which will concern Mr. Krajisnik which it is only sensible to have properly discussed between him and his counsel before he starts his evidence. It's -- I don't know exactly how long it would take in the nature of things, one doesn't know, Your Honour. But it's bound to be more than just a very few minutes, that's -- based on very long experience of discussions between counsel and Mr. Krajisnik, that's bound to be the position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that most of the issues, since they are -- well, I would say there are limited changes to the previous two after that, you have anticipated a kind of decision going approximately in this direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a mixture. We anticipated some things, some things we didn't, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Some things we would have liked differently, so the usual mixture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you would need some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say more than a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It will be inevitably, Your Honour. We do -- after all, we do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, certainly it can't be significantly less than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not asking for hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on one particular aspect, and this is the question of communication, just perhaps useful to make it clear so that Mr. Krajisnik can hear this as well straight away. We had anticipated this, but we'd anticipated wrongly as it happens. We had discussed and specifically indicated to Mr. Krajisnik yesterday how we thought he would communicate a need to talk to us. And we had suggested -- after all, we had to answer the question from our own common sense and anticipation. Your Honour, we had suggested that he would simply say in open court in everybody's hearing if he wanted to communicate with us and then would publicly say -- well, as little as was necessary to indicate why he wished to communicate with us. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have chosen this procedure, Mr. Stewart, in order to give full respect to client/counsel privilege. It could be there is some matter which should not be heard by the Prosecution; therefore, we introduced this system in which the Prosecution of course is only aware that there is a request. But if you would suggest if Mr. Krajisnik would address us in open court and tell us: I'd like to have communication with counsel for those and those reasons, of course it would come down approximately to the same. So I'm -- I'm quite willing to consider with the -- with my fellow Judges to see whether if Mr. Krajisnik has no problems in giving information about the reasons why he wants to see counsel or why he wants to speak to counsel, that we give him an opportunity where it's immediately translated so that we don't have to wait for the written translation. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that may very well -- thank you for that, Your Honour, because that may very well be an immediately flexible, practical approach and save trouble --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be an alternative procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We -- we specifically, of course, reminded Mr. Krajisnik that if we had adopted the procedure which I just outlined, that it would be public, it would be communicated to the Prosecution, and therefore he should bear that in mind in what he said. Your Honour, perhaps one might bear in mind this, that so far as - and no disrespect intended, Your Honour - but so far as Mr. Krajisnik, or we on his behalf, had misgivings about what he should communicate to the Prosecution, with the greatest respect, the same misgivings might apply in relation communication to the Trial Chamber, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We are not particularly happy, I do want to make that clear on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, with the aspect of the procedure Your Honour outlined where a communication goes from Mr. Krajisnik to the Trial Chamber and then according to the order which is made at the moment is then kept between Mr. Krajisnik and the Trial Chamber and not communicated to even the Defence. So, Your Honour, most of the time, if Your Honours would approach it in the flexible manner that has just been considered in the last few minutes, most of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- We would have a preference for Mr. Krajisnik simply to make that announcement there and then in brief terms in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- I will then move now to the short agenda. First of all, we have the submission of the requested Nielsen source material. After no agreement was reached by the parties regarding the submission of that source material, this Chamber has on the 27th of March has ordered the Prosecution to submit the communications received by the Presidency. The Chamber informed the Defence that they would have two weeks from the date of submission of these documents to raise any objection. Mr. Stewart, you've stated on the 11th of April that the two weeks that I had indicated for a response from the Defence have expired, and I announced that we would decide on the matter but we'll not receive that material this afternoon, and that was on the 11th of April. The materials were not yet submitted. The two weeks for the Defence to object have not yet begun to run. And, Mr. Harmon, I would like to invite you to submit the Nielsen material and then remind the Defence that they have two weeks from today to raise any objections. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was a matter addressed I think at the last court session. At that time Prosecution indicated that we had available the binders in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're prepared to tender them, but I think we ran out of time. The Defence also has the materials -- has had the materials for quite some time included in the three binders I believe which -- which contain not only these materials but the additional materials to which we've made reference during the discussions of this matter about this matter. So we have the materials in court, we can give them to the Court now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like you to submit them today and the two weeks start from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good. We'll provide them to the registrar at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have -- as the second item on our agenda, we have the exhibits introduced during the testimony of Witness D24. We had the minutes of two Presidency Sessions. These minutes were tendered by the Defence on the 10th of April. That is Session 21C dated the 2nd of August, 1992. And Session 32 dated the 29th of September, 1992. These items, as far as we remember, have not been assigned exhibit numbers. When these exhibits were tendered, the Defence has stated that the documents were obtained by investigators working on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik and promised that it would do its best to make inquiries as to the provenance of the documents. The parties also need to be given an opportunity to raise objections to items introduced and to make submissions on which items, if any, should be admitted under seal. The Chamber stated that it would decide on matters of admitting under seal and referred specifically to D170, which is a letter from Krajisnik and Mr. -- Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic to Ambassador Cutileiro. First of all, Mr. Registrar, could you assign exhibit numbers to the two Presidency Sessions minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D174 for the August 1992, Your Honours, and D175 for September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the Defence inform the Chamber, meanwhile, by the provenance of these documents apart from that they were obtained by an investigator working on behalf of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can't provide any further information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- at this moment. Your Honour, I wouldn't go so far as to say that I promised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But we will continue to try and answer this particular inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is, in your expectation, would be the time in which you could perform that task? I mean, if we leave you without dead-lines, I know -- I'm just as human as you are. You know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The answer to that question is -- if I focus my mind on it I don't need very long, because I'm going to either get some help -- useful information or not. So a week would suffice, frankly. I -- as a result of the e-mail exchange yesterday, I asked for it to be done again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Should we give you time until Friday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this is a first of a number of matters that might require discussion with our client. So that's the one caveat. Let's assume that it doesn't and that we get the information from the investigators and I feel I don't need to discuss it with Mr. Krajisnik. If I do, I'll mention that to the Court. And it will, frankly, have to wait. I hope that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you first focus on -- I take it that you know who the investigator is. We're just asking about provenance without any further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you get it from whom and then you have the next chain in the -- so but there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There aren't many candidates, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then until next week Friday --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you have time to provide that information. Then the next issue would be whether there are any objections to exhibits and whether there are any submissions in respect of admitting -- admission under seal of those exhibits you've tendered through Witness D24, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, D170, I submit, does not need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D170 not under seal. Any other exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Court will have to excuse me. I don't have a list in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. When could you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Later today. I will not need to speak to Mr. Krajisnik about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We expect later today to give further -- to receive further information as to whether there's any wish to -- for protective measures in respect of any of these exhibits. Mr. Harmon, as matters stand now, any objections? Or Mr. Tieger, I don't know who to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can defer, Your Honour, our objections, if any, until we hear from the Defence further on this matter. I need to check on one item on these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Josse will inform us by the end of this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will inform us by tomorrow -- oh, you will inform us by today. Then perhaps no need to say that -- and of course we could not expect any -- any positions to be taken by the Prosecution on documents that were not yet translated, missing English translations for the Defence are D171, D173, the two Presidency Session minutes which meanwhile have received D174 and D175. And there's no B/C/S translation yet for D170 you would like to be admitted under seal, Mr. Josse, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I said it doesn't need to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm -- I'm sorry, it's the beginning of the week. Let's blame the beginning of the week for it. You said "not under seal," but a translation is still not there. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then for the Prosecution P1166 needs to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we're aware of that, Your Honour. It's being translated as we speak, and we will have the translation, we hope, within a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Same applies, Your Honour, to D1168, which is noted on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- the transcript now says and I heard you also saying "D1168," but it should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1168, yes. This is as far as the exhibits introduced during the testimony of Witness D24 is concerned. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal with the matter now. The registrar very efficiently has provided me with a list. I am very grateful. The Defence submit that D171 and D173 should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you, Mr. Harmon, about the confidential character of D171 and D172 whether there's any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I said "173," Your Honour. 171 and 173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard, and that's what I intended to repeat but I misspoke. Then Mr. Registrar has received the compact disk regarding the Tuzla convoy but no number has yet been assigned. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D176, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D176. But we have not received yet any transcripts. Are they being prepared or do they exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They do not exist, Your Honour. These are items that were given to the Defence because the Defence felt these were important. We don't believe the transcript is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the -- is it just the visual impression that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The position is as I previously stated and is rightly summarised in the e-mail exchange of yesterday, namely, the Defence do not consider it a worthwhile use of our resources to provide a transcript. I regret to say the Chamber will have to watch this video in silence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, that's not always bad to do something in silence, Mr. Josse. We'll do that, so that means that admission of D176 is limited to the images and does not include any sound. It -- I'll not be tempted to do otherwise because I take it that it's not understandable for me anyhow, so as it will not be for my colleagues. Yes. Then the next issue is the double pension legislation. The matter was raised during the testimony of Mr. Poplasen's testimony -- the testimony of Mr. Poplasen. And we have requested the parties to submit the text of the legislation from whatever side. On the 28th of March, the Prosecution indicated that copies of two pieces of pension legislation had been provided to the Defence, and we've given you - I think you it was you, Mr. Josse - another week to discuss the matter with the accused. On the 10th of April, you informally indicated that you were not ready yet at that time to submit the legislation. And on the 17th of April, you indicated that in a communication that you were translating relevant sections of a different Republika Srpska statute and requested more time, and the Prosecution has asked for the citation of this legislation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, more material on this subject arrived from Bosnia last week. That, frankly, has not been looked at by any member of our team for reasons which I hope are understandable. And I spent some time, the earlier part of last week, discussing this with Mr. Krajisnik, and I could -- I would be prepared to provide the citation of the legislation that we believe is also applicable in the Federation. Having said that, how far that will take matters, I don't know, and as I've already just stated, the new material has not yet been looked at. I repeat again what I said in my e-mail of yesterday, this is a subject which our client takes a keen interest and would, no doubt, wish to discuss with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you need more time. At the same time, the Prosecution has provided some material. Could we start by just deciding on the admission of the Prosecution -- the material the Prosecution has provided. It's legislation, it's not a very subjective matter, although, of course, it needs interpretation. And let's also keep in mind that legislation and pension benefits can have all kind of different reasons to be adopted. I'm aware of pension legislation which not necessarily reflects a situation of hard work, even if the period in time would be covered by pension. So therefore, let's not make that perhaps the vital issue on the matter. But of course we should look at it. But I then suggest that we invite the Prosecution to submit whatever legislation they have and give you some additional time to see whether the Defence would like to submit other material on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I've no objection to that, Your Honour. The time-scale, though, is a difficulty, bearing in mind that Mr. Krajisnik is going to be -- commence his evidence very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, and perhaps that's one of the issues you could briefly discuss with him. At the same time -- first of all, in the interpretation of such material of course you could say we could speak with Mr. Krajisnik at length after he's finished his testimony. Of course you could ask Mr. Krajisnik questions on the matter during his examination, even if you would not be fully briefed we will hear what his position as far as this legislation concerning this would be. So therefore without giving any expectation as far as whether this would be such an expectational matter which would create a need to discuss these kind of matters -- I mean, we're talking about legislation, we're not talking about another witness statement or testimony given at another moment or -- I mean, it's a piece of legislation which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will try my best. As I already stated, I have no objection to my learned friend's documents being handed to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon -- then as far as time is concerned, how much time would you need to look at the new material? Would until the -- well, 9th of the May, would that be a suggestion to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the 9th of May is the dead-line given to the Defence to submit any further material. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. We have done the following. We have, based on Mr. Poplasen's evidence referencing double pension legislation, we have gone to legislation dealing with pensions in both the Federation and the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They are extensive pieces of legislation. One has 253 articles, one has 157 articles. We have not bothered translating the complete set of legislation in both of the entities, nor have we made copies of these. What we have done is we have identified the relevant provision that was identified, first of all, by Mr. Poplasen in the Federation legislation. And based on court inquiry during the colloquy with the parties as to whether or not there was a equivalent provision in the Republika Srpska legislation, we surveyed that legislation and identified an equivalent, what we submit is an equivalent article, or articles. So we have identified those, we have translated those, and we will be prepared to submit copies of only those articles. If the Court wishes, we can also make copies and submit untranslated the complete legislations in both of the entities dealing with the pensions, but I leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then be very practical. The Defence has received copies of the, in your view, relevant portions and the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then, also until the 9th of May, give the Defence an opportunity to add any article of this legislation which in the Defence's view would be relevant, then seek translation to be made so that what finally will be received by the Chamber are those articles. So that means the heading, law of this and this state, et cetera, et cetera published there, there, and there. And then the relevant articles, relevant both in view of the Prosecution and the Defence, and we would like then to receive any suggestion for adding articles to the translation also by the 9th of May, Mr. Josse. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next item on the agenda is the retranslation of P824 and submission of Official Gazette. We asked you, Mr. Harmon, to submit a retranslation of Exhibit P824, tab 1, which is a decision of the Serb Assembly of Hadzici municipality, and to submit, if it was available to you, the Official Gazette number 11 of 1992 containing a decree on the return of the Serb Republic -- to the Serb Republic of the people who moved out, which is referred to in the Assembly decision and to provide that to us by the 30th of March. And as far as our recollection goes, we have not received it. Could you update us on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed, Your Honour, that we will need one more week to complete that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, is there any problem if we would grant an additional week to the Prosecution to finalise this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not as far as the Defence are concerned, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you got the week you asked for, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- yes. There is a matter which has to be dealt with in private session, number 5 on the agenda, Mr. Josse. I see you nodding. I don't know yet whether it's yes or no, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, for my -- our part it does not need to be dealt with at this stage in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll leave it as it is for the time being unless you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am basically agreeable with what Mr. Zahar has suggested. If the need arises, then it will be revisited, as Your Honour has indicated, somewhat later in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that means that the three exhibits mentioned here, that's P595, P596, and P597, will remain under seal, and we'll hear from the Defence if there's any need to change that, and then we'll hear that in private session and then we'll give a decision. But as matters stand now, we leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't need to spend any more time on it. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got two matters. One tiny and one not very big. The tiny matter is this, Your Honour. In paragraph 15 of Your Honours' order yesterday it doesn't happen everyday in this case, but I've been given undue credit there, Your Honour. The detective work was not done by me, it was done by my co-detective, Mr. Josse, who spotted the error. I'm the person who brought it to your attention, yes, but I was just the messenger. But the credit for that eagle eye belongs to Mr. Josse. The second matter is this, Your Honour. It may be helpful just now for one moment before Your Honours adjourn. May I just show Your Honour and the Prosecution and everybody else just very, very briefly what we've done by way of presentation of material and the hyperlinking, because then if Your Honours had any questions that occurred to you over the short break, then it might be helpful. I've got Mr. Sladojevic beside me. He can bring up on Your Honours' screen now a list of the various folders. Okay. Do Your Honours have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a practical problem, perhaps that's the first question I would have, that my screen is -- and I see that the same might be true for you, Mr. Registrar, that it's very vague, as a matter of fact. It's almost impossible to read, and that seems to be a technical matter rather than anything else, unless I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it seems a good job that we are dealing with this now then, Your Honour, so we can see whether we can iron out some of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There must be something in the connection which makes it a bit blurred rather than -- and now we have it right on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's maybe a different button or something like that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, do Your Honours see now clearly, I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they're pretty self-explanatory. We've got -- well, it's about 17 files, because there's folders, there's A and B. The matches that Your Honours will see 14, some have got an A and B number, but 14 folders and then equivalent what are referred to as binders. And if Mr. Sladojevic, for example, were to bring up any one would do, actually, say 6A would do, Republika Srpska government sessions, Your Honours will see the list there and the hyperlinking English and B/C/S. For most of us in court it will be English, well, most or all of the time. I'm not proposing -- it's not technically feasible anyway, actually, Your Honour, not proposing that we double up by some of us using the English hyperlinking and Mr. Krajisnik, for example, using the B/C/S hyperlinking. That really won't work. But it won't matter. Mr. Krajisnik can be provided and will be provided with hard copy of anything in B/C/S -- well, it will be B/C/S in his case that you want to ask him about if there is the need, as there is sometimes for Your Honours and everybody else to look at the B/C/S document to see what it looks like, then we can bring it up by hyperlinking in this way. May I just add, Your Honour, that not a great deal of this material is in evidence, quite a bit of it tucked away in the recesses of P64, Mr. Treanor's 28 binders, and good luck to anybody that goes foraging in those binders. But there's quite a lot of stuff that isn't in evidence. Your Honour, may we just approach it this way, that from time to time we perhaps review what should go in evidence and what is not in evidence. But we hope that this is -- Your Honour can see from the nature of the material, we hope this is a practical help to all concerned in getting through Mr. Krajisnik's evidence as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that any material that's not yet in evidence that we receive that in hard copy as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Any material that's not in yet evidence, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. That we receive it if it will be introduced during the testimony. You may have noticed that now and then I try to browse --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have spotted that occasionally over the past two years, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I, in fact, continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'm not asking Your Honour to break the habits of a lifetime or two years. Your Honour, yes, I just hope that -- excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's no problem. I'm always anxious to preserve us from massive multiple copying jobs. But, in principle, yes, of course, Your Honour, and we wish Your Honours to have that material in usable form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That looks promising, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I hope the promise will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a computer addict, but at least as someone who sees the advantages of using electronical material so that you have quick access to the material we have to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to acknowledge in advance the extreme help from Mr. Sladojevic and other members of my team in putting this together. That means they get the blame if it goes wrong, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter, apart from this tiny one and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's done, Your Honour, those two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assuming that it will be a possibility for you, Mr. Stewart, and you, Mr. Josse, to confer with Mr. Krajisnik during the break, we'd like to give you 37 minutes and re-start at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour, that's our break gone. It's -- Your Honour, it -- well, that's our break gone. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have during the last five weeks or six weeks, I have never had a break without at least two or three meetings, so I'm aware that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to make a point, Your Honour, I have a whole team and, Your Honour, it's a reasonable request, actually. This has been -- these have been pretty hard days for my team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll start at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to call its next witness which I do understand is Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not quite, Your Honour. As a result of the discussions which -- thank you for giving us the opportunity of having with Mr. Krajisnik, there are a few points which the Defence wishes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would like to raise before --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they -- some of them arise out of the order, Your Honour. Actually, may I deal with the tiny points first. Mr. Krajisnik would like to take the -- this is not a big point, Your Honour, the earphone with which he is familiar and comfortable, the one-ear earphone. He would like to take that with him into the witness box. We don't see a major problem about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I. I do not see any objection from my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, also Mr. Krajisnik in the light of Your Honours' decision as it stands at the moment, Mr. Krajisnik would like to have, if possible, the videotapes. Your Honours' order refers to the audiotapes. He would like to have, if possible, the videotapes which obviously includes the audio of his evidence each day as quickly as they can be made available. On CD because that's the -- I said "tapes," I'm using that rather loosely, Your Honour. These days they come on CDs or DVDs that are playable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. We'll look at how quickly they can be produced, and we'll further consider whether there would be any objection against it. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just -- I may say, Your Honour -- sorry. Your Honour, I just had in mind it seemed a clear implication of Your Honours' order and the reference to audiotapes that they would be provided as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- the Judges have no problems but of course we would have to inquire into technical possibilities. Of course, one of the major advantages of DVD above anything else is that you can more quickly go through the material and move forward more easily and at the same time look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would be possible, then we would certainly support that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I understand it, Mr. Krajisnik doesn't have the facilities to view tapes, Your Honour, so that's why that specific request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next matter is the matter of the -- Your Honours will recall the letter, the recent letter that Mr. Krajisnik had delivered to the Trial Chamber on the question of witnesses and a suggestion of interference with Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it was returned. The position, Your Honour, as far as Defence counsel are concerned, Your Honour, is that we have no filing ready, prepared in any sort of draft on that matter, and we have to inform the Trial Chamber and Mr. Krajisnik that it is by no means -- and by no means sure that there ever will be a filing on that matter by counsel on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf. Mr. Krajisnik is, once again, insistent, that's his word, which I pass on to Your Honours, he is once again insistent that he wishes that letter of his to go to Your Honours. Your Honour, I really can - and I hope Your Honours -- I really can do no more than pass on that message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand the discussion between counsel and the accused have been finalised by now and we'll see what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The last point, Your Honour, is a matter of very considerable concern to Mr. Krajisnik, and therefore I also make this point from him. He has had drawn to his attention and has considered what Your Honours said in your order in relation to the timing of the final briefs, filing of final briefs, where Your Honours said that -- the fact that counsel for the Defence have not found time to work on the brief, that's during the course of the case, may be due to Mr. Krajisnik's non-payment since the start of the trial if his assessed contribution to his Defence fund, which is a significant portion of the whole, and we informed him fully of that paragraph and Your Honours' expressed view that you should not give the Tribunal's precious time to compensate for his decision to keep his Defence team underfunded. Mr. Krajisnik wishes me to communicate from him to the Trial Chamber that he considers that he has met all the obligations which he undertook from his discussions with the Registry at around the time hat I came into the case in the summer of 2004. So he does -- well, he rejects that point in Your Honours' order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But at the same time, Mr. Stewart, you're well aware -- I do understand that you communicate to the Chamber what Mr. Krajisnik's position in that respect is. It is more or less commenting on the Chamber's decision, and you know what -- if you do not agree either with the reasoning or the outcome of a decision what is the proper way of doing that and that would be to consider whether it would merit an appeal or not and rather not to give your -- to express your feelings of unhappiness with the decision or the reasoning of it is not a very common thing to do. But I do understand that you are at this moment, which is the last moment in which you could do it for the time being, that you're communicating to us the feelings of Mr. Krajisnik in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour understands very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- where we are on that. Your Honour, in relation to -- and accepting what Your Honour has said about the proper mechanism for certification appeal and so on, of course we're fully aware of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To consider whether it merits, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I -- yes, I didn't say anything different, Your Honour. Agreed, Your Honour. The -- so far as the -- I know Mr. Josse wants to have a word in a moment, and I will ask for that opportunity in just a second. But so far as the final -- preparation of final briefs are concerned, again it's for consideration whether an application is made for certification of appeal, and we have Mr. Krajisnik's view on that, Your Honour. He wishes us to express now, though, his extreme dissatisfaction at a timetable which, for practical purposes, he feels -- and on this, Your Honour, the Defence does support this last point by way of submission, he won't have an adequate opportunity to participate in the preparation of the final brief himself, especially having regard to the language difficulties which, of course, in relation to that particular item in that particular timetable are especially difficult, to put it mildly. So we do -- we do make that point, Your Honour. May I have a moment? I know Mr. Josse wants to have a word with me about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's it, Your Honour, for -- on all those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a question whether you're ready to call your next witness, being Mr. Krajisnik, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is my next witness, Your Honour, and I do call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Krajisnik, yes, you would like to raise a matter? You are raising your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judges, maybe I didn't ask quite well, but I had asked Mr. Stewart to notify you that I wanted him to appeal a decision as a precondition for an appeal based on the fact that I didn't participate in my defence. So I wanted your decision on which made conditional the submission of a motion. I wanted that appealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not fully understand. Are you saying to us, Mr. Krajisnik, at this moment that you instructed Mr. Stewart to appeal against the decision we delivered yesterday? Is that what you are -- yes. Well, then, we'll hear from Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart knows --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the part that concerns my participation in the financing of the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I explained to you that -- you say the reasoning is incorrect. I now fully understand that you instructed Mr. Stewart to seek a certificate for an appeal focussing on that portion of the decision that is the reasoning for not granting additional time for preparation of your final briefs where it says that it may be due as well to -- yes. I do understand. Since this is the very last moment that you could express yourself on the matter in a communication with Mr. Stewart, that you would like to emphasise that. Mr. Stewart, I take it the matter is clear that Mr. Krajisnik told us that he instructed you to seek a certificate for an appeal on this specific matter, and we'll hear from you or in a -- in the near future about it. And of course, Mr. Krajisnik, I cannot make any assessment on what could cause Mr. Stewart either to follow your instruction or to be hesitant to do so. And if that would need further discussions, Mr. Stewart or you will ask us for further communication on the matter before Mr. Stewart will file the appeal. I can imagine that it's a matter which needs further attention, but the Chamber stays out of it. But you clarified what Mr. Stewart told us is that you did not only express your dissatisfaction with that portion of the decision, but that it is your wish that a certificate for appeal will be applied for. That is clear at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Trial Chamber will be able to see very well areas here arising out of this order and in connection with this order which involve a distinct conflict of interest between counsel and client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not conflict, but conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Although conflict of interest can, of course, lead to conflict quite easily. Your Honour, frankly, we were -- we were troubled by the timing of this order. However it happened, the effect was that after having what was going to be for the foreseeable future our last meeting with Mr. Krajisnik yesterday at the -- yesterday afternoon at the Detention Unit, that actually sometime later in the course of our evening's work picking up the order, we've now had to deal - and thank you for the time earlier, Your Honours - but we have now had to deal with an order involving a number of different points which Mr. Krajisnik has not got in translation, though we have very skillful interpreters on our team. I'm concerned, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik and I, I'm happy to say, we parted on very friendly terms yesterday evening when Mr. Josse and Mr. Krajisnik and I and all concerned, we left the Detention Unit and that friendly tone has persisted this morning. But I -- I'm -- I do not feel comfortable about embarking on Mr. Krajisnik's evidence if there is, as there sometimes is then, lingering tension, lingering misgivings on Mr. Krajisnik's part, given that I as his counsel now have to examine him in chief for some considerable time. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm asking for, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not -- please proceed. I was about to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon, Your Honour. Thank you so much. I would ask for a few more minutes with Mr. Krajisnik now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the -- and Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber has considered the matter. It's -- I mean, the potential conflict of interest is there. Of course, if the matter could be resolved by a short conversation, that would be fine; if, however, the apparent problem would not be resolved, the Chamber is thinking more in terms of seeking advice from a not directly involved counsel in the matter rather than anything else. The Chamber is not inclined to allow any further delay of the start of the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I ask for clarification, Your Honour. I've -- because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the matter -- the matter whether a certificate for appeal should be sought, yes or no, and for what reasons, I mean there still is an opportunity to separate that more or less from this case and seek someone to be involved who could advise Mr. Krajisnik on the matter and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I'm so sorry. That as the matter on which I sought qualification. A not directly involved counsel. Mr. Krajisnik is to have advice from someone else, is he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there is -- I understand -- let's say it in plain terms. I do understand that the matter of Mr. Krajisnik contributing to his own defence, to the costs of his own defence, might be a matter on which you have different views than Mr. Krajisnik has.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And different interests as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And different interests as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, one could consider to provide -- to provide, on a temporary basis, advice to Mr. Krajisnik by another lawyer whose task would be restricted entirely to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To -- sorry, Your Honour, to which matter, to the question of whether he should appeal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- sorry, Your Honour, that, with respect, that simply won't work. We are his counsel. We conduct his case. We either appeal on his behalf or we don't. I must say, Your Honour, I think we're going down some road where some other counsel involved starts lodging appeals on matters in a case which we are conducting on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf where we have a -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I feel the need to see this through, but I'm just wondering where on earth that goes. You see, it comes back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an incident in a -- a smaller incident -- of course the result is important both for you. You're seeking to have additional time to prepare for the final brief, Mr. Krajisnik has an interest to further time -- to seek further time for the preparation of a final brief. But he is mainly concerned about the reasoning of the Chamber, or at least a small part of the reasoning of the Chamber, and I can imagine that one of the matters of concern would be that you would not support entirely the criticism on that part of the reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- it's quite a complex issue, Your Honour. I should say that -- again, I don't believe for one moment there's anything improper about me saying this. I wrote on Mr. Krajisnik's instructions to the Registry on his behalf in relation to this matter recently, but it has now been agreed between the Registry and me and -- the Registry and me in not any collusive way that it -- because of this potential conflict it's not appropriate for me to continue that correspondence. Mr. Krajisnik is free to correspond directly at any time with the Registry and they of course with him, and on the particular issue it's been understood that I really -- it is my suggestion that I really needed to step aside from that. But, Your Honour, there are -- there's -- I won't go into it, Your Honour, but Mr. Krajisnik's assertions about his agreements and arrangements with the Registry back in 2004, those are factual matters in which I was not directly involved. I was, of course, very heavily involved in the whole question of my coming into the case naturally and all sorts of financial aspects, but they involve, if you like, factual matters on which I have nothing to say because I wasn't there at particular discussions. But they do give rise to a conflict. But what also -- and, Your Honour, may I mention this. What also causes enormous difficulty and a real conflict of interest between counsel and client is that where Your Honours, for example, in this latest order say that one of the reasons why we, counsel, haven't been able to work on the final brief during the course of the case may be Mr. Krajisnik's failure to make his contribution, we have already summarised this submission before. The possibilities are all or any of a combination of failure to make his combination, inadequate work by counsel, or excessive pressures on counsel of the case. And the non-identification of which of those ingredients contributes to the difficulty and an order in this form which says that this may be a reason and then goes on to make an order based on the footing that it is part of the reason puts me and Mr. Krajisnik in a terribly difficult position. And what I'm concerned about, Your Honour -- I said it not cryptically, but I said I had Mr. Krajisnik's views on the question of certification and so on. It's now clear what those views are. A, they have to be very carefully considered; but B, the time for certification is going to tick away, or an application for certification is going to tick away, and it's going to expire in about seven days' time. So it's going to expire right in the middle of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence. That's not going to be easy, Your Honour, if Mr. Krajisnik is not happy with our decision, let alone Your Honour's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we -- of course we could extend the time-limit if we want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That puts off the evil day, Your Honour, but that doesn't solve the problem one tiny bit. It makes it worse, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it does, Your Honour, because then it's ticking away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll discuss the matter for most likely approximately 15 minutes at this moment. You have an opportunity to speak to Mr. Krajisnik on the matter. And one of the things --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would just like you to consider as a possibility, Mr. Stewart, is the following. I was at a point earlier to explain to Mr. Krajisnik the difference between a decision, a criticism to a decision, and a criticism to the reasoning of a decision. If you -- if you say: I'm not happy with the reasons, that does not necessarily result in another decision. Sometimes reasons can be replaced by other reasons. We've really considered the matter, so that is a matter. One of the things I could imagine - and that's perhaps I was not very precise in my wordings, and I do agree with you that it's a complex matter - one of the things I had in mind that if you're both seeking more time, and if you find there are good reasons to do so and therefore you would be inclined to seek certification of the -- for an appeal, and if Mr. Krajisnik wants to go in the same direction, that as far as the reasons for the appeal are concerned, one could imagine that you in your request for a certification, you would write down all the reasons you consider reasonable reasons for such an appeal and add to them, very specifically, to say: I add to these reasons reasons I'm instructed by my client to give for such an appeal, leaving apart whether I would or would not fully support but I accept these reasons on the basis that he was advised by a qualified lawyer on this matter and therefore I adopt those reasons in my appeal. That's a way of manoeuvreing through the problems which I would not consider at first sight to be inappropriate and I'd -- it doesn't have a great impact, I take it, on the way the appeal is handled or the request for a certificate. I would just like you to consider that possibility and perhaps, if you have considered it and if you think it worthwhile, to discuss it with Mr. Krajisnik, to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will certainly give it consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We will adjourn for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is there -- has your conversation with Mr. Krajisnik changed anything compared to the position before we left this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it -- it hasn't changed anything in substance. We've -- we have discussed various points, Your Honour, and there's a measure of agreement on some things and then there are other matters unresolved. But what it has brought us to is this, Your Honour, and this inevitably has to be an assessment by Mr. Josse and me as well as a submission. But, Your Honour, we do not consider that Mr. Krajisnik is in a state to begin evidence today. Mr. Krajisnik agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having consulted by colleagues -- first of all, is -- does the Prosecution wish to add anything to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber decides that we will start in a couple of minutes from now on the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik, which has been prepared for such a long time. Secondly, for a better understanding of our decision delivered yesterday specifically on the subject matter of the dead-line for the final briefs, the parties are informed that the reasons for denying the time asked for preparing final briefs are found in paragraph 19 of that decision. If a request for a certificate for an appeal would be filed, whatever we'll find in that request the Chamber will in any case consider what Mr. Krajisnik told us about his dissatisfaction on paragraph 20 of the decision. This is the ruling of the Chamber. Then the Defence is now requested to call its next witness, which is Mr. Krajisnik, so that he starts his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I call Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to follow Madam Usher to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I see that you have now your own earphone with you. And before I'll invite you to make a solemn declaration, I'd just like to inform you and inform the Defence as well that we inquired into the possibility of providing you with a DVD. It's possible to prepare a DVD so that you can review that, video DVD, but it takes a bit more time. It would cause a delay of approximately one day, so where an audio CD or DVD could be provided within -- well, let's say within one hour, this would take 24 hours. So I take it that you still prefer to have the DVD -- the video DVD. Is that correct? Yes, I see you are nodding yes. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, you're now in a different position, not only I would say geographically, you're not anymore on my right-hand side, you're just in front of me. That means you are in a different position. You will now become a witness in your own case. And the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have some paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what are your full names, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, have you -- have you brought with you into the witness box or in your case a copy of what you know to be a draft 89(F) statement. It's 44 paragraphs and it's something which you have, yourself, made some handwritten amendments to overnight?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I brought it. May I take it out of my brief-case? I have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it you want to submit it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, you are invited to do so, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the way -- and the Prosecution have been informed of this, Your Honour. Because Mr. Krajisnik has made some amendments overnight, there are quite a few of them, though they are quite short, and as I did notify the -- an officer in the Trial Chamber early this morning, we wish to have this read into the record. The procedure I would propose to adopt, Your Honour, is that I would read from the English, and I do know on which paragraphs Mr. Krajisnik has a change to make, and I would then give him that opportunity paragraph by paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to add that in B/C/S so that it will be translated and it will be in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. And then no doubt in due course we can get something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, this is your statement which I'm going to ask you whether you confirm in the end, Mr. Krajisnik. That: "I was born on the 20th of January 1945 in Zabrdje, a suburban community in the Sarajevo metropolitan area. My father was Sretko, my mother, Milka. I have one brother, Mirko Krajisnik, born in 1950." Paragraph 2: "I attended elementary school in Reljevo not far from Zabrdje. Then I attended economics middle school in Sarajevo from 1959 to 1963. I completed my studies at the faculty of economics in 1967 and took my degree on the 2nd of October, 1968. I completed my graduate studies in 1975 in Sarajevo and later successfully defended my master's thesis in 1980. My brother, Mirko, went to the same middle school and later also was graduated from the faculty of economics in Sarajevo." Paragraph 3: "As a student, I was not politically active on campus, but I was a member of the youth organisation and the SSRN, Socialist Alliance of Working People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those organisations were created by the communist regime but had no independent political weight and were under the control of the communist party. In this way, I had the opportunity of representing the Zabrdje area. As I was rated an exemplary youth, I was accorded the privilege of serving my military duty in 1969 to 1970 in my native city of Sarajevo. After the normal few months of boot camp, I remained in Sarajevo in the post of commander of a unit which was training a new batch of raw recruits at the reserve officers school educational centre. I was first employed on the 15th of October, 1968, at the Energoinvest enterprise in Sarajevo. I was assigned to the financial services section of the company, Energobanka. I was employed there until 1975 except for the 11 months I spent in military service. Until I was called-up I was a clerk. After my release from the army and two years of on-the-job training, I was promoted to director of the financial services section. After Energoinvest was reorganised, I was transferred to the TAT" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Director of the service in a big sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was director of a service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Promoted to director of the ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: A service, but a sector is high above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, before Mr. Stewart continues I don't know if he heard but perhaps it would be helpful to provide --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear, thank you. And I apologise. I thought it had happened. Do the interpreters want both the B/C/S and the English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reading might take some additional time, so if there's any way of copying -- if -- if any copies are available -- of course we have an English version but not a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, my apologies. I'd only like to say that there have been terrible problems out there in the Defence room today with broken-down photocopiers, printer not working, and so on. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's any need -- if that would instruct any further problems, then I would invite those who are supporting Chambers to make, quickly, copies as soon as we have received a B/C/S and an English version. I take it that production will take --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah, we can give a B/C/S version immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the English copy is there as well. The Chamber's support staff will take care that within a couple of minutes copies will be there so that the interpreters will on from then have no further difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please, if you would proceed then at this moment at a low speed, as you had already, reading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After Energoinvest was reorganised, I was transferred to the TAT Termoaparati factory in Sarajevo which was an integral part of Energoinvest. I was financial director of the factory. After TAT was reorganised in" -- and I think you want to make a change to this bit, Mr. Krajisnik. "After TAT was reorganised in 1977, I became one of the vice-presidents of the business committee in charge of finance." And you wish to make some change to that last sentence, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I just wish to add something, that this reorganisation was carried out. Now was it 1976 or 1977, I'm not sure, but your associates have already entered the correction, that I was vice-president of the business committee in charge of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So the -- it's just that the date -- it can read: "After TAT was reorganised in 1976 or 1977," and then as the text stands?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 5: "In 1973, I married Milanka Micevic, who was born in 1949. She was a teacher and worked at the Reljevo and Brijesce elementary schools close to Zabrdje. My wife and I lived with our children in our own house. I lived in Zabrdje from birth to the beginning of the war in April 1992 when I moved with my family to Pale. My wife and I had three children: Milica, born in 1974; Milos born in 1978; and Njegos born in 1982. All were born in Sarajevo. Milica, Milos, and Njegos were all graduated in economics, the last being Njegos on 28 March, 2006. All three studied in Pale and are living there now." Paragraph 6: "I first met Radovan Karadzic in 1983. At that time I was employed at TAT while Dr. Karadzic was a psychiatrist at the Sarajevo clinical centre. Dr. Karadzic was working part time at the Energoinvest medical centre in downtown Sarajevo about 6" - sorry, my mistake - "about 10 kilometres from the TAT main office which was in Stup in the municipality of Ilidza. I met Dr. Karadzic by chance in 1983 through a mutual acquaintance. That acquaintance asked me to help a friend of his, meaning Dr. Karadzic, by giving him professional advice on how to obtain credit for the construction of an industrial facility." And, Mr. Krajisnik, I think there may be a change at the very end there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. This is a combined facility, business and housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, exactly how you would wish it to read then, that sentence, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: To obtain credit for the building of a combined business/housing facility. That is, a facility that is used for residential purposes and for production, small-scale production.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, if we add on at the end then that small explanation, that is a facility that is used for residential purposes and for production, small-scale production, and it can read in that way? Thank you. Paragraph 7: "The three of us, my friend, Dr. Karadzic and I, met in a Sarajevo restaurant called Snack Bar in the Malta district. I explained to Dr. Karadzic what types of loans were available from the various banks. I was in a position to do that because as part of my job I was dealing with most Sarajevo financial institutions on an everyday basis. Dr. Karadzic was finally successful in obtaining a loan, but I played no role in that nor were my further services required. I learned of these further developments from the mutual acquaintance. As a few months later, Dr. Karadzic began to work at the Energoinvest ambulance, I began to see him from time to time." And, Mr. Krajisnik, I think you do have some changes to make in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. After the word "Dr. Karadzic got a credit, obtained a loan," it should be added -- or rather, the following words should be added. "By investing his own foreign currency." That was the easiest type of loan to get. And at the end of the paragraph: "He worked as a freelancer in Vares or Breza," I don't know exactly which town," in addition to working at the Energoinvest infirmary."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Paragraph 8: "Through Dr. Karadzic I met Nikola Koljevic, as he and Dr. Karadzic were long-time friends. These developments were taking place immediately prior to the Sarajevo Winter Olympics in 1984. Dr. Karadzic wanted to use the structure he had built to service Olympics visitors, but that did not come to fruition. Later on in 1984 Dr. Karadzic moved to Belgrade and spent half a year or more there. Being unable to resolve some personal issues, exchanging his Sarajevo apartment for one in the capital and finding a job there for his wife, Dr. Karadzic returned to Sarajevo to work at the same clinic where he had been employed before." And, Mr. Krajisnik, I think there may be a very small amendment to be made somewhere in that passage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I wanted the following to be added. For the apartment not to say capital but to say Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So it just reads: "Exchanging his Sarajevo apartment for one in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then going to the last sentence: "I was unaware at the time that Dr. Karadzic had moved to Belgrade or what the reasons were for that move. There as no contact between Dr. Karadzic and me while he was in Belgrade." Well, it wasn't the last sentence, but that's clear to you, that paragraph, is it, is it, Mr. Krajisnik? Thank you. You nodded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 9: "During our acquaintanceship Dr. Karadzic and I did get together socially such as for family visits or for holidays." Paragraph 10: "Until the first half of 1990, I had taken no part in politics or in any of the activities of which I was unaware anyway which led to the founding of the SDS party." And again I think there may be changes to be made to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think that something should be deleted. The part that's in brackets should be deleted and the following words should be inserted: "But on television and through the newspapers I followed, like any other citizen, what was going on on the political scene."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- those are all the changes to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik, are they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 11: "My family had been living in Zabrdje and Rajlovac over the previous 300 years. My father's property that Prosecution investigator Mr. Jovanovic had identified in Rajlovac and Zabrdje had been acquired by generations of Krajisniks. The only thing done by me personally was to construct a home, but part of the land it was situated on had been acquired by my parents." Paragraph 12: "Other than the home and the land, I had no other property in Zabrdje and Rajlovac. The property I held in Pale was acquired on credit and continues to be under encumbrance." Paragraph 13: "I first became involved in politics when I became a member of the SDS at the time of its founding on 13th of July, 1990." But, Mr. Krajisnik, you may have a change in that sentence? Which is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Instead of the 13th of July it should say the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So continuing. "At that time the SDS was a broad Serbian national movement which Serbs were joining en masse. I was not on the SDS founding committee, nor did Dr. Karadzic insist that I join. I don't know why I wasn't asked to join. It was probably because Dr. Karadzic was aware of my aversion to active involvement in politics and because there were other people who were involved whom Dr. Karadzic had known better and for longer." Paragraph 14: "Until late September/early October 1990, I was not in any sense active in SDS politics. I did not attend a single SDS election rally prior to the November 1990 elections. Specifically, I did not attend rallies in any municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Sanski Most. Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Koljevic did attend those rallies. The only political meeting I attended was in my native community when the SDS candidates for parliament for Sarajevo were being introduced to the voters." And, Mr. Krajisnik, again I think you may have some changes to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, the words "and others" should be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that the only change to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After Sanski Most the following words should be added, which was stated by one of the Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What are the words, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Including the municipality of Sanski Most, behind that the following should be added: "Which was stated by a Prosecution witness," meaning Sanski Most, that I attended an election rally in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Under -- well, clear, as a matter of language surprising. Thank you. Paragraph 15: "I joined the SDS as a regular member, as many Serbs did who saw the SDS as the only legitimate Serb political movement, in response to the formation of the Muslim and Croat nationalist parties, the SDA and HDZ, respectively.
