I had intended to devote myself to my business responsibilities at TAT, where I enjoyed widespread support among employees after my exoneration. I wanted to do my best for the enterprise as a gesture of appreciation to the workers who stood behind me when I had been charged and put on trial with Dr. Karadzic and others in 1985 and finally acquitted about four years later." Just to clarify, Mr. Krajisnik, when you talk about support among employees after your exoneration, you are referring to that point in the next sentence, are you, your eventual acquittal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. In 1984 proceedings were initiated. I was suspended from my job, and towards the end of 1989 I was returned to the same job thanks to the workers. And then I owed them, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then paragraph 16: "I also wanted to devote myself to my family and sick wife." Paragraph 17: "I first became actively engaged in politics sometime in 1990 when I was asked by the SDS main office, not Dr. Karadzic, to appear as an SDS spokesman in a Radio Sarajevo programme to explain to listeners the SDS economic programme. Each political party, SDA, SDS, and HDZ, was to have a representative on the programme. The caller explained that the person originally scheduled to appear had pulled out due to cold feet for fear of losing his job if he raised his political profile. I accepted on the condition that I never be asked to perform a similar favour again. Dr. Karadzic was unaware of my being asked to appear on the programme." Mr. Krajisnik, you may have changes, I think, to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the second line. After the words that are under quotation marks "SDS headquarters," the following words should be added: "I do not remember who called me." And finally at the end in the brackets where it says: "In order to appear in the programme," the following words should be added: "At least that's what I think," meaning that I did not know whether Dr. Karadzic was unaware or not but I thought that he was unaware.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then paragraph 18: "A short time after that radio show, there was another similar call asking me to appear on TV. The caller was Aleksa Buha, whom I did not know at the time. Buha asked me to speak on the same topics on television. I reiterated the condition under which I had agreed to appear on Radio Sarajevo. Buha said that the organisers of the TV debate had failed utterly and that the party were desperate to have a competent spokesman to explain their position. I agreed because I did not want the SDS to be unrepresented in the economic debate but said that this would really be my last appearance. In fact, the SDS did not have much of an economic programme and I mostly articulated my own views on the need for privatisation and other reforms." Paragraph 19: "After that TV show, Mr. Buha called me again asking me to make another television appearance. This time I resolutely refused his request on the grounds of our last agreement that the last appearance would really be the last one and that I had a forthcoming business trip on behalf of my company. While on my business trip, I watched the TV programme that I had been asked to participate in, and to my surprise there was an empty chair where the SDS representative should have been sitting, which I felt guilty about." Mr. Krajisnik, I think you may have changes to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Line 3. When it says "categorically" here -- or rather, "resolutely," I think that should be deleted. And this business trip to Trebinje. It was to Trebinje that I went to. So I think that should be added, "to Trebinje."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 20: "Upon my return to Sarajevo, I called the SDS main office and spoke to Mr. Buha. He told me that the original economic spokesman was still too frightened to appear. I felt bad about this and told Mr. Buha that if ever the party needed someone to explain its economic position they could count on me. After that, I was called upon to be a guest in two or three TV debates." 21: "About a month before the elections, I was called by the municipal committee of the SDS for Novi Grad, the most densely populated district of Sarajevo. I attended a meeting that evening which turned out to be the first meeting of the district SDS committee. There was a great deal of dissension among those present and some heavy criticisms from the representative of the SDS Main Board. I asked for the floor and addressed those present with some conciliatory words which helped to reduce tensions. To my surprise, at the end of the meeting Glavonjic took the floor and proposed that he resign and that I replace him." Mr. Krajisnik, you may have a change to that paragraph, I think?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After the word "chairman" it should be said is that this is the chairman of the initiative board of the Serb Democratic Party of the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then paragraph 22: "I wholeheartedly rejected this suggestion and it failed. I did not hear it at the time but later learned that Glavonjic had said that it would be reconsidered at the following meeting." It's not clear to me, Mr. Krajisnik, whether you have any change to that paragraph. Do you or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There is no need to amend this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. 23: "At the next meeting a day or two later, Glavonjic reiterated his proposal. I was still firmly opposed to entering into politics. After the meeting, I nevertheless consulted my wife and parents. As fate would have it, the political fever was infecting most BiH citizens, including my own family. Political broadcasts became the subject of widespread interest which the public was following intensely. Neither my wife nor parents opposed the idea. They left it up to me to decide." Mr. Krajisnik, I think you will have a change?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After the words "wife and parents," the following text should be added: "Whom I had promised that I would not become politically involved, and if the situation would make it incumbent upon me to do that I would ask for their consent regarding that decision of mine."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 24: "At the next SDS district meeting, approximately one month before the November 1990 elections, Velibor Ostojic was in attendance. I did not know Ostojic before then. Ostojic spoke calmly and kept control of the meeting. He said that his mission was to make sure that a local SDS chairman was elected. The consensus of those present was that it should be me. I kept declining and even pointed out that I had spent time in prison, which might damage the party's reputation. Instead of concern, those present welcomed that fact and said that was a plus, because it showed that I was a dissident who had been persecuted by the communist regime." Mr. Krajisnik, do you have changes to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like two amendments to be made. After the words in the -- in line 4, "control of the meeting," the following words should be added: "As opposed to his predecessor." And at the end of this paragraph the following text: "That is how I became the chairman of the initiative committee of the municipality of Novi Grad" -- or rather: "The initiative committee of the SDS of the municipality of Novi Grad for the period up to the elections."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Those are all the changes to that paragraph, are they, Mr. Krajisnik? Well, you've waved --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You have to say yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 25: "Soon thereafter, the issue of candidates for the two chambers of BiH legislature arose, the Chamber of municipalities and the chamber of citizens. Since the chamber of municipalities candidate had scant chances of electoral success because of the local ethnic composition, which was only 27 per cent Serb, there was not much competition for that candidacy, but disagreements did arise once candidates for the other chamber came up for discussion. There were two factions, one promoting myself and the other some other candidate. I refused to stand and nominated somebody else. Views became polarised. My suggestion that they should focus on nominating a good candidate for a leading post in the Sarajevo municipal government did not ease the tension. In order to calm passions, I finally agreed to be a candidate on the metropolitan level. Unkovic was the first candidate, while I was his running mate in the number two spot who did not have much chance of winning." Mr. Krajisnik, I think you may have changes for that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Line 4, there was not much commotion. I think the word "commotion" should be replaced with the word "discussion" or "debate." In the next line after that where it says one of them supported me, it should read "supported my nomination." And after that where it says: "The executive authorities of the Sarajevo municipality," it should read: "The executive authority of the City Assembly." There is a difference between the municipality and the Municipal Assembly or the City Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Can we clarify, Mr. Krajisnik, the -- what would -- for the purposes of the English, apart from anything else, you said that in line 4 of your text that the word "commotion" should be replaced with the word "discussion or "debate." What we have in English, I think that's the passage you're talking about, was: "There was not much competition for that candidacy." Are you saying that it should read: "There was not much discussion," to choose one word, "there was not much discussion about that candidacy but disagreements did arise." Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That explanation in English sounds correct. There was no competition and there was no great debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I feel confident we can tidy that up, Mr. Krajisnik. Thank you. Paragraph 26, therefor: "The two-candidate formula that was agreed to was sent to the city SDS committee for approval. Throughout this time I had no dealings with Dr. Karadzic or any other city committee functionary. I have no idea who moved for my name to be placed on the Sarajevo electoral list. Nobody had ever explained that to me. In the end, my name was number six on the overall SDS list of candidates." 27: "In November 1990, I was on the list of deputies from the Sarajevo region. I did not participate in a single pre-election rally except for the one in my own village or town where I lived, Rajlovac, as well as the final convention when all deputies' candidates for Sarajevo gathered in the Vasa Pelagic Hall in Sarajevo. I also participated in one radio show as well as about four TV broadcasts." 28: "In the first electoral round, the SDS gained five seats in Sarajevo, which means that I was not elected. I made it subsequently when electoral results were assessed according to a formula and parties which failed to gain a minimum of votes were eliminated from consideration. In that redistribution, the SDS gained an additional seat and that is how I was elected." 29: "After the elections, the victorious parties divided up political spoils and the post of president of parliament was allocated to SDS. SDS was promoting the candidacy of Milan Trbojevic for that post. I was present while Dr. Karadzic and Trbojevic were discussing it and was aware that that was party policy. Dr. Karadzic conveyed that decision to Trbojevic and Trbojevic accepted that position." It's slightly ambiguous in English, Mr. Krajisnik. It's -- the sense in Serbian must be - is this right - that Mr. Trbojevic accepted the situation as Dr. Karadzic reported it to him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic offered to Mr. Trbojevic the candidacy for the post of Speaker of parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Mr. Trbojevic accepted it. It should have been a done deal, at least that's what I understood at that meeting between the two of them which I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I choose the position there, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm going to move on. Number 30: "I became a candidate for the chairman of the Executive Committee of SDS for the city of Sarajevo. This time I did want the position and accepted it willingly. I wanted to use it to help my native communities of Zabrdje and Rajlovac which were rather neglected in their development in spite of their central location within the metropolitan area. No one told me that I was going to become candidate for Speaker of the Assembly." 31: "Dr. Karadzic was pushing for a Sarajevo candidate and spoke out strongly in favour of Mr. Trbojevic. When Trbojevic's candidacy failed, a call was put through to me at home to attend an expanded meeting of the Deputies' Club." 32: "Due to a misunderstanding with Mr. Ostojic, I barged into the session of the SDS Executive Committee and then angrily returned home. When I reached home again, I found a message asking me to return immediately to the meeting I had just left." 33: "They directed me to the meeting of the Deputies' Club and I found them engaged in a fierce debate about who should be the party candidate for parliament president. Members of the SDS city committee were rebelled against the official choice for parliament president. They objected that Mr. Trbojevic would be just another Sarajevo man in high office and that this would be unfair to the Krajina region since most candidates had a Sarajevo background. There was an influential group of deputies that demanded that Mr. Trbojevic's candidacy be rejected and that he be replaced by a candidate from Krajina (i.e. a 'Krajisnik')." Is there a change that you wish to make to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: An addition should be made after the word "Sarajevo background," "on which point I think the deputies were right." That should be the addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 34: "I knew hardly any of those present except for Radovan Karadzic. Dr. Karadzic came in and asked for the floor. He said - and this is almost verbatim: 'Some of you want our candidate to be a Sarajevo man, others want a Krajisnik, so I now give you a Krajisnik from Sarajevo.' The deputies were perplexed and they started asking what my name was. That is how I came to be elected, because of my surname and place of residence." Is there any change you wish to make to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After "Dr. Karadzic," I assumed there was someone else as well and perhaps somebody else as well. I have -- I only saw Karadzic, but I assume there was somebody else in addition to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where -- perhaps you could try and be precise about what words you would wish to go into that paragraph and where, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Line 1 should read: "I knew none of those present except for Radovan Karadzic and maybe one other person who rose and asked for the floor." So the addition is actually: "And maybe one other person." I knew very few people, but it wouldn't be true to say it was only Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you wish to leave in or take out the short second sentence: "Dr. Karadzic came in and asked for the floor."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No. I only wish to say this: "Except for Radovan Karadzic and one other person who came in and asked for the floor."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 35: "Before that, no one, including Dr. Karadzic, talked to me about this candidacy. That was a complete surprise for me, and I had no ready response. I was elected first candidate to the post and then president of BiH parliament." Do you have some change to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I had, but I gave up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The translation was "give up." You're positive you do not wish to make any change?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I give up on the correction that I had indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 36: "Although the original plan was for me to be elected member of the SDS city executive committee, I ended up president of parliament without having played any role in the process. I formally became parliament president at that body's session in November 1990." Any change to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Two changes, actually. In line 1: "Although the initial plan," instead of "original plan." And in the penultimate line -- sorry, line 2. Instead of: "Member of the Executive Committee," it should be: "President of the Executive Committee."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 37: "I did not participate in the creation of the SDS at the BiH level. Although I was then president of the Zabrdje SSRN (Socialist Alliance of the Working People), I did take part in forming the local SDS in Zabrdje and Smiljevic (two small communities) and I announced that my mandate was about to expire due to the creation of the multi-party system and the first multi-party elections. During this farewell meeting, it was suggested to those assembled to express their views as to which party they wanted to see formed. The people of Zabrdje and Smiljevic decided to choose a party by voting. Due to the fact that almost 100 per cent of the inhabitants of these two communities were Serbs, they opted for the SDS. That party then became embraced as the movement of the Serbian people. The decision was adopted after the SDS was formed on July 12, 1990. I do not recall the precise date, but it must have been shortly thereafter." Do you have any change to that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Behind the part of the sentence where it says: "Due to the fact that almost 100 per cent of the inhabitants of these two communities were Serbs," that should be corrected. Not all the people from Smiljevici and Zabrdje were Serbs, but all the people or almost all the people at that meeting, at that rally, were Serbs. That was the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 38: "Citizens didn't elect the president of the organising committee but, rather, asked me to set up another meeting, which I did, thus helping them to form the Zabrdje branch of SDS. I was then invited to take part in the work of the organising committee for the Sarajevo municipality Novi Grad. I learned subsequently that the reason for this invitation was the result of a disagreement in the Novi Grad SDS Municipal Board. The parties in dispute literally forced me to accept the position of the organising committee Presidency and to remain in this position until the next elections, which I did. During my mandate, I didn't have contacts with the party leadership. I didn't wish to get involved politically, nor did anybody invite me to do so. What occurred was but a conjunction of circumstances." 39: "Since the circumstances were different, I did take part in SDS electoral preparations in Novi Grad. I was granted a special status and treatment by members of the SDS Board because I was extremely busy with work at my firm and because of my wife's illness. For those reasons I was not involved to any great extent in the preparations that lasted for about a month." "After the signing of the Dayton Agreement, I headed the commission for its implementation on the Serbian side. "From 1996 to 1998 I was elected member of the Presidency representing the Republika Srpska. In order to become a candidate for this position, I was subjected to all of the checks deemed necessary by international supervisors." We're talking there, aren't we, Mr. Krajisnik, of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 42: "While a member of the Presidency, I met with numerous international representatives, including presidents of the most influential countries in the world (former Prime Minister John Major, Prime Minister Tony Blair, former President Bill Clinton, President Kohl, President Jacques Chirac, Russian Prime Minister Chernomirdin, et cetera." Paragraph 43: "After 1998 and until my arrest in 2000, I was in private business. 44: "I was arrested on the 3rd of April, 2000 on the basis of a sealed indictment." The statement stops there, Mr. Krajisnik, and you have -- you were brought straight away to The Hague and you have been detained here in the United Nations Detention Unit ever since April of 2000. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik. Your Honours, the sensible course seems to be for us to have that typed up to reflect Mr. Krajisnik's changes. And then, if we may, when that's done then give it back to him in that typed up form and then he could, assuming he is then happy with all those amendments, he could then sign that typed up version. Would that suit Your Honours and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be a reasonable course to follow. So therefore you -- you will produce an amended version now in accordance with the amendments made. Mr. Krajisnik, the translation will be prepared and we'll finally ask Mr. Krajisnik to sign that copy. Apart from that, it is already on the record because it has been read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So even without signing the same would be true and it could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. We're not trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if one could wonder whether it's necessary at all, since all the words have been read and all the amendments. But perhaps it's good to have a document which reflects the original text and all the amendments made by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. It would seem to be good practice. Your Honour, since I -- well, I believe it's going to be necessary to have a break between when we came back and when we finish. Would Your Honours think this was the right point to have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the matter is whether we need another break. I'm looking at the technicians and the interpreters. Because we had a break 40 minutes relatively early. Then although I announced 15 minutes' break, that took a little bit over half an hour, and as far as the tapes are concerned, I think we could continue until quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I remind Your Honour that we have all been here all that time, that during what may have been a break actually most of the people have actually been here all that time. I don't want to appear to be weedy about it, Your Honour, but again it's the same point, both Mr. Krajisnik and my team. The interpreters are entitled to their breaks, but everybody will have gone a very long time by quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first break was not 37 minutes but 47 minutes finally, upon your request, the second break was announced for 15 minutes. That makes a total of one hour and two minutes, which is more than usual during the morning. I do understand that you are busy during the breaks, where the -- I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The total of the breaks this morning will be one hour and 12 minutes. We'll have a break of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you recall that in May 1991 you were invited on to a television programme in Sarajevo called Club 91?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that -- it was a one-to-one interview of you as the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina for quite a long time, an hour and a half, something like that, political interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have -- we've got a DVD of the interview. We aren't for one moment suggesting that we play it for an hour and a half. What we are proposing to do, Your Honour, is to play it for just a very few minutes so that Your Honours can see it, can get the flavour, and then of course we have the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have transcripts. You prepared transcripts of those portions or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of the whole programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll play only smaller portions. And I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wasn't even going to ask, but of course I'm in the -- if the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution -- the Prosecution have submissions or the Trial Chamber, I wasn't going to ask even to play the portions that I wish to refer to. The Defence's position is that it would be quite adequate for Your Honours just to see the first few minutes, to see the format, the flavour, because it doesn't really change, Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course the -- if the Prosecution would be of a different opinion, then of course if the atmosphere of the flavour would be different than any other portions, they are free to play whatever --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have no resistance whatever, Your Honour, to other parts being played if anybody -- but we do not propose that that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: "Dear viewers, good evening. This is Club 91 and, as you have heard, our guest this evening is Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Welcome and thank you for coming to Club 91. You have a masters degree but we rarely hear about it. You have a masters in economic sciences. Is that so? "Krajisnik: Yes. "Presenter: You are a man who started his career in Energoinvest where you worked for many years? "Krajisnik: Yes. "Presenter: "An Energoinvest man, old and loyal, I would say ... 17 "Krajisnik: Yes, both a loyal and old Energoinvest man. "Presenter: You were not involved in politics before, at least not in a very active way. Or were you? "Krajisnik: Well, if you discount that I was a member of the Socialist Alliance, an Assemblyman in the City Assembly, I was not particularly involved in politics until this election as deputy in the republican Assembly. "Presenter: And now you are president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at this time. Tell me, what was your personal motivation in accepting this exceptionally responsible and difficult post in these difficult times? "Krajisnik: Well, this is probably difficult to explain. It is more to do with man and his nature, and I wanted in these difficult moments to be a member of my people. And as things turned out, I wanted to be only a member of the Serbian Democratic Party and simply to participate as a human being as much as I would be able to help. And then one thing happened after another, and I didn't want to be a deputy and especially not the president of the Assembly, and everything happened more or less suddenly and more or less against my will. But that is the kind of man I am. So when I am committed to something and when I am elected by someone, or when they show me confidence, then I want to justify that. "Presenter: You are one of those republican officials who, it seems to me, as far as I have contact with people and information about that, who has been accepted by the public with quite a lot of understanding and sympathy. And in that respect I think that there are no particular national divisions about you. I think that your reputation has been growing with the number of sessions that are broadcast which often confuse the public, but few people refrain from complimenting you on your patience in chairing these sessions. I am trying actually to ask you this: Should the parliament look the way it looks? Is the criticism justified that their discussions, not to say arguments conducted there are pointless, or that that is simply a type of parliamentary debate that we are not used to and which possibly prevails everywhere in democracy?" "Krajisnik: Well, as regards your assessments" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could a number be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be for the video. And D177A for the B/C/S -- do we have a B/C/S transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D177A for the original B/C/S transcript and D177A.1 for the English translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, two minor matters or practical matters. The transcript in English that Your Honours have, it does occasionally say on it, there's an example at the very top of page 2: "Handwritten note in the margin of the last paragraph in English: Election as deputy and President of Assembly." Do Your Honours see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the explanation of that is that this was submitted for translation by our case manager who had made some relatively modest notes on the document. So of course in the entirely proper way the translation service translated -- if it doesn't move, translate it, they translated everything. Your Honour, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the -- the copies you would provide to the registrar, that this will be taken out, perhaps by a marker or something like that. And then -- then you provide a B/C/S original without these comments as well. And I don't think that there's any need that it will be reproduced seven or six times. It's clear to us now that whatever refers to any handwriting is work product which should not be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, that's very practical. Your Honour is absolutely right, it is very clear actually where these notes come up, and they're actually pretty harmless, it seems, but we didn't want to be hiding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar has not received yet the B/C/S copy. Could it be provided to him later today or at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we've got -- subject to any photocopying difficulties in the back there, we can do that. No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, you will be provided with D177A in B/C/S today. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've done one other practical thing, which we hope will have the Trial Chamber's approval, which we propose to adopt quite frequently. In order, as quickly as possible, to go to the relevant passage in the B/C/S version when I'm examining from the English version, I have taken the liberty of numbering, and for my own private purposes I do it on my copy, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, the points which I'm going to go to, and so the B/C/S has just numbers, Your Honour, at those points in the text in the margin with no other comment, no other marking, just the number, so I that I would, for example, say to Mr. Krajisnik: Can you find number 1 in the margin? And that will take us quickly to that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would then refer to us so that we can add on our own copies in order to better be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, for -- if it would ever come to that point, if ever an Appeals Chamber would have to consider this evidence, I would like you to add those numbers on the originals but not asking for any further translation, though that's handwriting, but that should remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we have one copy and that it's easy for everyone to identify the portions on which questions are put.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in practice it becomes increasingly difficult to find copies without the numbers as time goes on, so they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That used to be a very handy instrument to get rid of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We will follow Your Honour's proposal there. What I'm not a hundred per cent sure about now, Mr. Krajisnik, is whether you have in fact got with you in the witness box that B/C/S transcript with those numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have them, Mr. Krajisnik? Yes, Mr. Krajisnik is nodding yes. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if the system is working you should be able to find the number 3 in the margin quite early on -- I'm sorry, the number 1, I beg your pardon, a simple system, in the margin. You're nodding. You've found that, have you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then for us, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, indeed, straight away. It's page 3 of the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's the first answer by Mr. Krajisnik right in the middle of the page: "There will probably be viewers ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do stop me straight away if you're not immediately following exactly where we are in the -- in the text. But I don't think it will be a problem for you. So short question from the presenter. It says: "You came to this post as a member of the SDS. It should and do you feel like the president of the Assembly ... of all deputies?" And then your answer, which I will read, Mr. Krajisnik: "There will probably be viewers who will not believe that I truly feel ... not that I am the president for everyone but that I do everything as if I am the president for every citizen in this Bosnia and Herzegovina of ours, in fact our Bosnia-Herzegovina people. That is to say, my activities are that I do not want to do anything that is particularly against the interests of any people. Because according to any principle, moral, according to ... as our people say, according to local custom, to do an injustice, that is, that is an evil which can feed only the person who really in their sound like does not feel what it means to do an injustice and what it means to have an injustice done to him. I therefore think that a man cannot do the job of the president of the Assembly and be at any post, any post in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if he does not eliminate everything that is party-based and do his utmost," that's a misprint in the English, Your Honours, it's got to be the single word: "Utmost objectively for all the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then we get one of those handwritten notes which should come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in particular there your expression that: "A man cannot do the job of the president of the Assembly and be in any post, any post in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if he does not eliminate everything that is party-based," did this approach, as you have described it there -- first of all, did that genuinely represent your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that position of yours, as you described it there, gain support from your SDS colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then do you see the number 2, just further down, further along? It should be very shortly after the number 1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For us where do we find number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's Krajisnik: "I'm of the opinion that at all times" -- I'm not always going to read the question, Your Honour, because it doesn't always help to do that and it speeds things along. "I am of the opinion that at all times my position as president of the Assembly must be clearly on the table, for any deputy to assess it and can give an objective opinion about it to see if I am working in a good way objectively, if I am president for everyone and so on ... Thus, at that moment and in the future, I would never want to be president of the Assembly if one of the partners primarily, was against, or if such a ... such hostility was created, with the criticism that I am not working in the way that God demands, is that right ... as for quality, I think, that at all times there should be an interest in the party itself that that be done by the person who knows how to do it the best. As for bias, everyone must decide on that. It is very ruinous in this democracy if we have in posts, any post in Bosnia and Herzegovina, people who think that it is solely their aim to protect their people through the party, exclusively without paying attention to some objective circumstances -- what is possible and what is just..." And then there is another handwritten note that comes out. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, when you say about six or seven lines into that answer you say: "I would never want to be president of the Assembly if one of the partners primarily was against ..." In referring to "the partners," who were you meaning?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Here I am primarily referring to the SDA and the HDZ, because I believe that the opposition can be against things even if I'm working properly. Because it is in the interest of the opposition to topple the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say -- further on in the same answer you say: "It is very ruinous in this democracy if we have in posts any posts in Bosnia and Herzegovina people who think that it is solely their aim to protect their people." First of all, did you have in mind any particular people who did at that time, in your view, think it was solely their aim to protect their people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At that time, as a rule, the representative of a party that was in government would think that it is in his interest only to protect the interests of his own people, his own ethnic group, not of all. But he actually represents all the peoples, the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims. What I meant here was that it would be ruinous if somebody were to be a candidate on behalf of the SDS or the HDZ or the SDA and protect only the interests of that people or that party. Everyone should do their job properly, and in that way they will protect the interests of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Within your own party, the SDS, were there people who, in your view at that time, thought it was solely their aim to protect their people, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That question, in a way, requires a more extensive answer, perhaps because it's somewhat equivocal. Every representative of the SDS thought that it was the Serb people who should be protected, but the SDA protected the Muslim people, the HDZ the Croatian people. However, in the SDS there were some extreme phenomena, if I can put it that way. Let things be good for the Serbs and let the others fare for themselves, but these people were a minority. The absolute majority supported the line that I advocated and that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are close to quarter to 2.00. Mr. Krajisnik, we'll finish for the day. I instruct you, as every other witness, not to -- you could perhaps even speak the words yourself, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given today and you're still about to give, not the coming days but the coming weeks. So that's the instruction, and we'd like to see you back then of course tomorrow morning in this same courtroom at 9.00. We'll adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
